exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```ruby
word = "ruby"
puts "#{word.upcase}#{word.length}" + '#{word}'
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Look at the quotes around the last string.

hints: Interpolation happens only in double-quoted strings.
exercises.solution: The double-quoted string interpolates `word.upcase` (`RUBY`) and `word.length` (`4`). The single-quoted string is literal, so it contributes the characters `#{word}` unchanged. Joined with `+`: `RUBY4#{word}`.

feedback.message: Close. `succ` is the successor: the next integer.

exercises.solution: `10.gcd(4)` is 2 and `7.succ` is 8, so the sum is **10**. Both are ordinary method calls on Integer objects.

options.label: `Class`
options.feedback: Yes. Classes are objects, and the class of a class is `Class`.

options.label: `Integer`
options.feedback: Not yet. `42.class` is `Integer`; we are asking about `Integer` itself.

options.label: `Numeric`
options.feedback: Not yet. `Numeric` is Integer's superclass, which you get with `Integer.superclass`, not its class.

options.label: It is an error, because classes are not objects.
options.feedback: Not yet. In Ruby, classes are objects too.

hints: Classes are objects too, so they have a class.
Superclass and class are different questions.
exercises.solution: Every Ruby value is an object, including classes. `Integer` is an instance of the class `Class`, so `Integer.class` is `Class`. Its *superclass* (`Integer.superclass`) is `Numeric`, which is a different relationship.

exercises.prompt: How many lines of output does `puts [1, nil, "two"]` produce?

feedback.message: Not yet. `puts` treats an array specially.

hints: `puts` prints each element of an array on its own line.
exercises.solution: `puts` prints each array element on its own line: `1`, then an empty line for `nil` (whose `to_s` is the empty string), then `two`. That is **3** lines.

exercises.prompt: A variable `x` might be `nil`, `""` or `"nil"`, and you want to see which while debugging. Which line shows the difference?

options.label: `p x`
options.feedback: Yes. `p` prints the inspected form: `nil`, `""` and `"nil"` all look different.

options.label: `puts x`
options.feedback: Not yet. `puts nil` and `puts ""` both print an empty line.

options.label: `print x`
options.feedback: Not yet. `print nil` prints nothing, just like `print ""`.

options.label: `puts "#{x}"`
options.feedback: Not yet. Interpolation calls `to_s`, and `nil.to_s` is the empty string.

hints: Which printing method shows values the way a programmer would write them?
exercises.solution: `p` calls `inspect`, which shows `nil` as `nil`, the empty string as `""` and the string `"nil"` with its quotes. `puts`, `print` and interpolation all use `to_s`, which makes `nil` and `""` look identical.
`255.to_s(2)` is `"11111111"`, eight ones, so its length is **8**.

exercises.prompt: Why do Ruby developers on macOS and Linux usually install Ruby with a version manager (rbenv, chruby, asdf or mise) rather than the operating system's Ruby?

options.label: Different projects pin different Ruby versions, and the system Ruby is often old and used by the system itself.
options.feedback: Yes. A version manager installs several Rubies side by side and switches automatically, often by reading a project's `.ruby-version` file.

options.label: Because the system Ruby cannot run `.rb` files.
options.feedback: Not yet. It can; it is just usually older and shared with the operating system.

options.label: Because version managers make Ruby code run faster.
options.feedback: Not yet. They manage which Ruby is installed and selected; they do not change its speed.

options.label: Because RubyGems only works with version managers.
options.feedback: Not yet. RubyGems ships with every Ruby.

hints: Think of two projects on the same laptop that need different Ruby versions.
exercises.solution: Real projects specify the Ruby version they need, and you will work on several at once. A version manager installs each version in your home directory and switches between them per project, leaving the operating system's own Ruby (if any) untouched.
